title: Microschool vs. Private School: A 2026 Comparison for Families
summary: Microschool vs. private school: compare size, cost, schedule, and teaching, with questions to help you decide which setting fits your child best
body_text: If you’ve started looking at options beyond your child’s current school, you’ve probably run into the term “private school” plenty of times. But you may be seeing “microschool” for the first time. For many families, one term is familiar and the other is brand new. So it’s worth getting clear on what each one actually means. “Private school” is a funding and enrollment category. It tells you how a school is recognized, not what it’s like day to day. “Microschool” is a model, defined by how small the group is and how learning is structured. Below, we compare the two on size, class structure, pace, schedule, teaching, and cost, so you can think through which setting suits your child. At KaiPod Learning, we support the largest network of microschools in the country, with 150+ founders across 30+ states, so we see every day what microschools actually look like in practice. We’re not here to argue that one model beats the other. Both can serve children well, in different ways. The aim is to help you ask the right questions about your own child. Here’s what we’ll cover: What families usually mean by "private school" What a microschool is How microschools and private schools compare Size and class structure Learning pace Schedule and flexibility Teachers and relationships What each model costs Questions to ask yourself about your child Finding a microschool near you You May Also Be Interested In What families usually mean by “private school” For most families, “private school” calls to mind a fairly consistent picture: a dedicated campus, structured grade levels, credentialed teachers, a set school day and calendar, a formal curriculum, and tuition. Private schools vary in size, from small religious schools to large independent academies. Across that range, class sizes typically fall in the mid-teens, around 14 to 16 students per class according to federal data . Whatever the size, the experience is generally modeled on what school has looked like for a long time. Children are grouped by grade and move through a standard sequence together, with progress reported through familiar report cards and letter grades. The main appeal of a traditional private school is predictability. A family usually knows what the year will look like, how their child will be graded, and what the path to the next grade or school involves. What a microschool is A microschool is a small learning community, often serving fewer than 25 children. No two are exactly alike, but most share a few features: Very small group sizes Personalized and often self-paced learning Multi-age groupings rather than fixed grades Flexible schedules A close relationship between the educator and each child If you want a fuller picture of the model, our guide to what a microschool is walks through it in detail, and how microschools work covers what a typical day involves. Educators in a microschool often describe themselves as guides or teachers rather than lecturers, working alongside small groups and tracking progress through portfolios, projects, and observation as much as through traditional grades. (In many states, microschools are legally classified as private schools, homeschools, or charter partnerships. That label is about funding and recognition, not size or teaching approach.) How microschools and private schools compare Here is a side-by-side look at the attributes families ask about most. Attribute Private school Microschool Typical size Medium to large Very small, often under 25 children Class structure Grade-level cohorts in traditional classrooms Multi-age groupings, not always fixed by grade Learning pace Mostly grade-based and standardized Flexible and individualized, often self-paced Schedule Fixed school day and school year Structured but flexible; some run hybrid schedules Teaching model Credentialed teachers in classrooms An educator or guide, with a smaller teacher-to-student ratio Cost Tuition required; national average around $15,000 a year Tuition required; most charge $10,000 or less Most of the differences come down to scale and structure. The sections below add a little context to the rows families tend to weigh most. Size and class structure The clearest difference is scale. A microschool keeps the group small and often mixes ages, so a child might work alongside slightly older or younger peers, grouped by skill in a given subject rather than strictly by age. For some children, a larger, more structured environment is energizing. For others, a small group where the educator knows them well makes it easier to stay engaged. The right fit comes down to how your child does in a room full of people. Learning pace Private schools generally follow a grade-based, standardized pace. Microschools tend to be more individualized, letting children move faster or slower by subject and proficiency. A self-paced setting can let a child move ahead in reading while taking more time in math, matching the work to where they actually are in each subject. Other children do better with a more standardized pace, where everyone moves through the same material together on a steady, predictable rhythm. The right pace depends on how your child learns, not on which model sounds better on paper. Schedule and flexibility Schedules differ too. Private schools run on a fixed school day and calendar. Microschools are often more flexible, and some operate on hybrid schedules of just two or three days on site. For families, that flexibility can be a deciding factor , especially when it helps with travel, outside activities, or a child’s own energy levels. It has less to do with how a child learns and more with how a family’s week fits together. Teachers and relationships Private schools usually staff classrooms with a 14 to 16:1 teacher-to-student ratio. Microschools run smaller teacher-to-student ratios, which is part of why the relationship between educator and child tends to be closer. Really, it comes down to how much individual attention your child needs to do their best work , and how much you value the structure a larger faculty can offer. What each model costs Both models charge tuition, and the cost ranges overlap considerably. For private schools, the national average sits around $15,000 a year, according to Private School Review , though that average hides wide variation. Elementary tuition tends to run lower, high school higher, and costs differ sharply by state. Microschools are usually less expensive. According to the National Microschooling Center , the typical cost to educate one child runs around $6,500, and most microschools charge $10,000 or less in tuition. Questions to ask yourself about your child A side-by-side comparison only goes so far. The more useful exercise is to think about your own child and what your family is looking for. A few questions worth sitting with: Does your child do best with a close, personal relationship with one teacher, or with finding their footing in a larger, more independent environment? Does your child learn best moving at their own pace, or with the structure of a grade-level curriculum? How much does schedule flexibility matter to your family? Are you looking for a school with established traditions, extracurriculars, and a recognized name, or a smaller community built around your child’s individual growth? Is your child engaged and challenged where they are now, or do you sense their current setting isn’t quite the right fit? There are no right answers here, and many families consider both options before deciding. Neither model is the better choice for every child. Microschooling is one path among several worth exploring. Finding a microschool near you If a microschool sounds like it might fit your child, the best next step is to see what exists in your area. Every microschool is different, so visiting a few is the clearest way to tell whether the size, pace, and community feel right. You can browse options on our microschool directory to find a school near you. Download the 2026 Family Guide to Microschools to get additional insights and recommendations about what to look for when you visit. title: A News Director for Science
body_text: Times veteran Russell Goldman will join the desk as lead news editor in September. Read more in the below note from Science editor, Bill Wasik. In recent years, desks at The Times have been encouraged to appoint a lead news editor: someone to serve as the main point of contact on news and work with the desk’s whole team, editors and writers alike, to find ways to make their daily coverage as urgent and vital as possible. I am thrilled to announce that Russell Goldman, a 12-year veteran of the International desk, has agreed to take on that role for Science, with the title of news director. For the past two years, Russell has been the International desk’s senior global news editor, helping to set the desk’s daily news agenda on many of the report’s biggest stories, including the wars in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran, as well as advancing the effort to make the report more live, visual and explanatory. Previously, Russell was a regional Middle East editor, helping shape the desk’s coverage of the most consequential events in the region, notably the Oct. 7 attacks in Israel and the war in Gaza. Russell also spent five years on the desk in Hong Kong, where he covered the protests that upended China’s decades-long governance of the territory. On January 23, 2020, he helped launch a live blog about the lockdown of Wuhan, China. He helped run what would become the Covid blog from Asia for the next 100 days. Before joining The Times, Russell spent seven years as a reporter and producer at ABC News, where he was the head writer of “Primetime Nightline” and covered the 2012 presidential election. In 2013, he was part of two ABC News teams that received the Edward R. Murrow Award for breaking news coverage of the Newtown, Conn., shootings, and the Peabody Award for coverage of Hurricane Sandy. In 2017, while working in Hong Kong, he shared the Award for Excellence in the category of Breaking News from the Society of Publishers in Asia. “Russell has always been a pacesetter for International, and for The Times,” said Phil Pan, the International editor. “He leads reporters and drives coverage creatively and urgently, because he understands how far we’ve come and how much further we have to go. He has a keen sense for news, audience and every kind of storytelling that can connect the two.” Michael Slackman, head of the News Desk, said: “Russell is the real thing. He has first-rate news judgment, enthusiasm for innovation, insatiable curiosity and a devotion to our mission. The Science desk is fortunate to have him.” In our conversations with Russell, he has bowled us over with his enthusiasm, his good humor and, above all, his ideas — he has a gift for looking around at the world and seeing questions that readers might have, and an infectious energy that makes you want to go find the answers. We won’t have Russell full-time on the desk until September, but in the weeks and months to come, he’ll be getting to know all of you, learning about your beats and starting to strategize about how we can build better processes and muscles for covering the news. Please join me in welcoming Russell to the Science desk! — Bill

title: A new era for surgery with real-time AI: Medtronic to unveil Touch Surgery™ Aide, the next-generation compute platform for the operating room at Society of Robotic Surgery 2026
summary: Advanced compute power, built on NVIDIA infrastructure, enables real-time decision support during the procedure FDA-cleared Instrument Exit Point (IEP), the first real-time AI application for...
body_text: Advanced compute power, built on NVIDIA infrastructure, enables real-time decision support during the procedure FDA-cleared Instrument Exit Point (IEP), the first real-time AI application for robotic procedures from Medtronic, advances a precise, predictable, and personalized future for surgery GALWAY, Ireland , July 21, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- Medtronic (NYSE: MDT), a global leader in healthcare technology, is presenting an early look at its next-generation compute platform for the operating room. Touch Surgery™ Aide — an AI-native surgical computing platform that powers the Touch Surgery™ ecosystem — enables real-time artificial intelligence during procedures. Touch Surgery™ Aide will be shared at the Society of Robotic Surgery (SRS) 2026 Annual Meeting in Florida, July 23-26. Built on years of experience, the Touch Surgery™ ecosystem brings insights to surgery, in more than 1,500 operating rooms worldwide. It connects the entire surgical journey: bridging pre-operative planning and training, intra-operative tele-mentoring and tele-proctoring, and AI-powered post-operative insights, simplifying workflows and extending access beyond individual ORs. Touch Surgery™ Aide expands the Touch Surgery™ ecosystem with next-generation computing capabilities, enabling multimodal AI-driven support during surgery. This provides surgeons with access to actionable insights during procedures, supports case review, and helps inform continuous improvement in clinical decision-making. "Real-time AI marks a new frontier for healthcare — it is a fundamental evolution in how surgery is supported, moving from technology that assists the surgeon's hand to technology that helps teams work smarter, move faster, and deliver greater impact in the moment," said Jim Peichel, Chief Technology Officer at Medtronic. Touch Surgery™ Aide incorporates NVIDIA's accelerated computing infrastructure, leveraging the company's Holoscan, CUDA, and TensorRT to deliver AI-powered insights in the moment, supporting surgical decision-making when it matters most. Touch Surgery™ Aide combines computer vision, multimodal AI, and accelerated inference to process surgical video and procedural context in real time. This enables multiple AI applications to run simultaneously during a live procedure, processing and acting on surgical data in the moment. It brings intelligent, increasingly automated support in the OR, and is designed to continuously learn and evolve. Medtronic's first real-time AI application for robotic surgery Instrument Exit Point (IEP) is an AI application that runs on Touch Surgery™ Aide, for use with the Hugo™ robotic-assisted surgery (RAS) system. It received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) clearance. Using computer vision, IEP provides a visual notification when select instruments move beyond the visible field of view during a robotic procedure. As the first real-time AI application to run on Touch Surgery™ Aide, IEP represents an early step in bringing AI-enabled support into robotic surgery, with the platform designed to support expansion into laparoscopic surgery over time. Medtronic continues to progress the capabilities of the Hugo™ robotic-assisted surgery (RAS) system. In December 2025, the Hugo™ RAS system received FDA clearance for use in urologic surgical procedures, bringing a versatile robotic-assisted platform to U.S. surgeons and health systems. In June 2026, Medtronic announced 510(k) submissions to expand the use of the Hugo™ RAS system into general and gynecologic specialties in the U.S. The Hugo™ RAS system continues to have a growing global impact and has been used in tens of thousands of procedures across more than 35 countries in six continents. Transforming the future of surgery This is an early step in a broader effort to bring AI into more of what happens in the operating room. Over time, Medtronic expects the platform to support a growing range of real-time AI applications, connect with other Medtronic technologies in the OR, and turn the data from every case into insights for surgical teams and the hospitals they work in. "Surgery is on the cusp of a generational shift, powered by AI and advanced compute," said George Murgatroyd, General Manager & Vice President, Digital Technologies within the Surgical business at Medtronic. "The Touch Surgery™ ecosystem, powered by Touch Surgery™ Aide, establishes a platform for a new generation of embedded connectivity, seamlessly integrating advanced capabilities into surgical workflows and reinforcing Medtronic's commitment to delivering the best possible care, for every patient, anywhere." About Medtronic Bold thinking. Bolder actions. We are Medtronic. Medtronic plc, headquartered in Galway, Ireland, is the leading global healthcare technology company that boldly attacks the most challenging health problems facing humanity by searching out and finding solutions. Our Mission — to alleviate pain, restore health, and extend life — unites a global team of 95,000+ passionate people across more than 150 countries. Our technologies and therapies treat 70 health conditions and include cardiac devices, surgical robotics, insulin pumps, surgical tools, patient monitoring systems, and more. Powered by our diverse knowledge, insatiable curiosity, and desire to help all those who need it, we deliver innovative technologies that transform the lives of two people every second, every hour, every day. Expect more from us as we empower insight-driven care, experiences that put people first, and better outcomes for our world. In everything we do, we are engineering the extraordinary. title: California American Water Advances $2.5 Million Well Rehabilitation Program to Enhance Water System Reliability
summary: California American Water is investing $2.5 million in its Northern District Well Rehabilitation Program, a multi-year effort to strengthen groundwater infrastructure, maintain well performance,...
body_text: SACRAMENTO, Calif. , July 23, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- California American Water is investing $2.5 million in its Northern District Well Rehabilitation Program, a multi-year effort to strengthen groundwater infrastructure, maintain well performance, and ensure safe, reliable water service across the region. Customers in the Northern District depend on more than 100 groundwater wells that require ongoing maintenance, rehabilitation, and replacement to support long-term reliability and water supply. The Well Rehabilitation Program includes upgrades at multiple well sites and will continue through December 2027. These efforts are intended to maintain groundwater production capacity and extend the life of essential water infrastructure. As part of the program, California American Water recently began rehabilitation at the Auberry Well in Sacramento's Parkway water system. Built in 1989, the well is being cleaned, redeveloped, and tested to optimize performance and improve long-term reliability. Work at the site includes inspections, pump removal and reinstallation, well testing, and condition assessments to enhance overall performance. "Regular well rehabilitation is an important part of maintaining a resilient and reliable water system," said Usmita Pokhrel, Senior Manager of Engineering at California American Water . "These investments help ensure our groundwater facilities continue operating efficiently, extend the life of critical infrastructure, and provide dependable service for our customers." Well rehabilitation may involve video inspections, cleaning, redevelopment, pump testing, electrical modifications, and other improvements to restore groundwater production capacity. Additional upgrades may include chemical treatment, freeze protection, equipment upgrades, and piping improvements, both below and above ground. California American Water coordinates rehabilitation activities to minimize customer impact and maintain reliable water service during construction. No service interruptions are expected as a result of this program. About American Water American Water (NYSE: AWK) is the largest regulated water and wastewater utility company in the United States. With a history dating back to 1886, We Keep Life Flowing® by providing safe, clean, reliable and affordable drinking water and wastewater services to more than 14 million people with regulated operations in 14 states and on 18 military installations. American Water's 6,700 talented professionals leverage their significant expertise and the company's national size and scale to achieve excellent outcomes for the benefit of customers, employees, investors and other stakeholders. For more information, visit amwater.com and join American Water on LinkedIn , Facebook , X and Instagram . About California American Water California American Water, a subsidiary of American Water, provides safe, clean, reliable and affordable water and wastewater services to approximately 750,000 people.
